title: Social Media Ad Sizes, Explained Simply | AIVideosUGC
description: Social media ad sizes for TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, and YouTube. Pick a tall phone video, a square post, or a wide screen, and make each file.
h1: Social Media Ad Sizes: Which Shape Goes Where
lead: Your ad fills the phone instead of sitting in a strip of black bars. For a sunscreen bottle, the tall file is the one that does that, with the tube in the middle, clear of the buttons.
secondary_keywords: square ads for the Facebook feed
summary: A small shop can cover a phone, a feed, and a wide screen without guessing the shape. Make the tall 9:16 file first for phone ads, add a square for the feed, and make 16:9 only when the screen is wide.

sections.h2: Which Social Styles Make a Shopper Stop
paras: The right style gives a shopper one clear reason to stop. Pick the style that shows that reason. The shape comes after the idea is clear.
A coffee lid that clicks shut can be the whole clip. Time that click to a track shoppers already hum, and end when the lid is closed. Pick a track they still hear this week.
A backpack clasp that opens with one hand is a better clip than a lecture. Show that one motion, and let the spoken line name it. Save a longer list of tips for a later file.
A lunchbox clip sells the moment the lid comes off at noon and the food is right there. Start on the open box, and let that be the whole file.
Answering a real question, like how it fits in a pocket, gives the shopper the detail they asked for. Show that, and keep the answer readable.

A shopper comparing two water bottles will pause for the lid, the weight, and whether it fits a car cup holder. Say those and leave the bottle in the frame the whole time. Another point can wait for a later file.
Watching the fill, the seal, and the unbox gives people a step they can trust.
Soft light and a real surface can sell the mood on your profile, often as a square. The label still has to match the product page.
One joke, then the product, easy to see. Keep the item in view once the joke lands.
Each placement gets a file that already fills its screen. Make that shape on its own, so the product stays large.
A wide YouTube screen gets a 16:9 file, and Shorts get a tall one that fills the phone. The tall file is its own job. See [YouTube Shorts](page:plat-youtube-shorts).

A square planter fills the scrolling feed, where people pass posts. The full-screen video placement and Stories want the tall file, and a square dropped into that tall slot leaves bars. Make the feed file and the tall file as two jobs.
A 9:16 file fills the TikTok screen, so the product stays large. A wide clip on an upright phone shrinks to a strip. Build the tall file with [AI UGC video ads](page:video-ads).
A square or a wide post gives people room to pause and read. Keep the words large, and keep the claim identical to the product page.

sections.h2: What Each Shape Keeps on Screen
paras: The product stays in the part of the screen shoppers can actually see. Match the shape to the screen, then check what the app covers. Confirm the crop in the ad manager. These are shapes, not a promise of one pixel size.
16:9 fills a laptop, a longer demo, or a desktop feed. A full phone screen wants the tall file instead.

9:16 is the tall shape, and it is the one that fills a phone. Account names sit at the top. Like and share sit on the right. Keep the sunscreen tube and any words in the middle, clear of those buttons.
1:1 fills a Facebook or Instagram feed, a swipeable row of cards, and the spots where the placement is still undecided. A still can use this shape too.

4:3, a little wider than a square, and 3:4, a little taller, fit the few placements that list them. When you want a shape the setup screen names, use 9:16, 1:1, or 16:9 for the rest. For current Shorts file rules, see [YouTube Shorts size rules](https://support.google.com/google-ads/answer/16041697?hl=en-GB).

paras: One coat photo can feed a tall file and a square file. They are two jobs, and each one shows its credit cost before it starts.
Opening on the cap, when other serum ads open on the dropper, gives your file a different first second. Use a track that still shows up where your buyers scroll.
You set the gap between the first word and the product, and that pace is yours. For a pour-over kettle, the gap might be one second. Put that gap in your own script.

You can post without standing on camera. Pick an AI actor from the [actor library](page:ai-actors), make one for the brand, or show only the product. Anyone on screen is an AI actor you chose for the shop.

The size and the color on a wool throw's product page can become the spoken line in a tall file, next to the photo you already took. That page is enough to begin. See [URL to video](page:url-to-video).
sections.alt: Adult woman with short curly hair holds a plain white sunscreen tube upright in a vertical social ad scene.

sections.h2: How Two Shops Split the Shapes
paras: A home shop gets a 9:16 file and a 1:1 file from the product page, instead of an evening spent cutting one video apart. They run the file that fills the placement.

A skincare shop gets a second opening for the same lip balm without a new photo. They keep the photo and the offer, change the first line, and run the two files for the same people on the same budget.

sections.h2: Which Style Fits the Product You Sell
paras: A pace that fits the product keeps the label easy to see. Keep the joke clear of the label too.
Beauty and skincare. A routine, a texture, or the surface before and after shows the shade in context. Hold the real item next to the screen and check the shade.
Fashion. Shoppers see the dress on a door and then worn, in the same color in both frames. Show the back when the photo you took includes the back.
Home. A shopper sees the room the piece belongs in, plus one close view of the joint, the cord, or the finish.
Food and drink. The pour, the steam, or the first bite is enough to show the product. Six or ten seconds often covers it.
Jewelry. A hand or a collar shows the piece at the size a shopper will wear it, with the clasp visible.
Gadgets. One motion, an earbuds case snapping shut, is enough to show what it does. Keep the words in the middle, where the buttons leave them readable.

sections.h2: What the Editor Handles for You
paras: The chores that used to mean three apps sit in one place.
You get an opening that fits the product, such as a candle flame in the first second, and a track that matches a slow shot. You still pick the line, and you pick one that fits this season.
A brand that never shows a face can still have a spoken line. Leave the frame on the product, and put that line on the caption track.
Cuts can land on a beat you pick from the ad music library. A spoon tap can sit on that beat.
A script you can edit. It is written from the product page, like a reply to a shopper. Change the line before the job starts.

A photo you already took of the cutting board is enough to start the clip. [AI image to video](page:image-to-video) is the way in. A product link is the other door, and it helps when the page has the size and the material written out.
Finish in one place. Captions, the spoken voice, and the song live in the editor. You can change how the words look, and you can make several openings from the same photo.
You spend your time on the shape and the line. The frame-by-frame trim is already handled.
A photo of the whole phone stand is the usual start. A product link works when the page already shows that stand. Bring a clip when you want the pace of something you filmed yourself.
Mark the second where the label has to be readable. The rest of the timing can flex around that second.
Pick one shape for this job: 9:16, 1:1, 16:9, 4:3, or 3:4. A second shape is a separate job.
The spoken line sits on screen in the middle, clear of the bottom and the right edge, where the app covers words. A song can wait until this pass looks right.
Download the file. Nothing is stamped on it. Play it on your phone before you pay to run it, and check that the product is still in the middle.
A video is 24 credits for 6 seconds, 40 for 10, 60 for 15, or 120 for 30.

paras: Three shapes cover the screens a small shop actually buys. Use 9:16 for full-screen phone ads, 1:1 for the scrolling feed, and 16:9 for wide screens. Use 4:3 or 3:4 only when that placement lists them. Keep the product in the middle.
A script, captions, a spoken voice, and a song can be included. A further shape is another job. If a job fails, the credits come back.

faq.q: Can a wide file become the tall phone version?
faq.a: Yes. Make the tall version as its own job, with the words placed for a phone. Watch that tall file before you retire the wide one.

faq.q: Can I post without showing my face?
faq.a: Yes. Keep the frame on the product and use a spoken line, or put an AI actor in the shot when the ad needs a person.

faq.q: Are the music and the spoken voice safe to use in an ad?
faq.a: Yes for the tracks in the music library and for the voice this product generates. A track you brought from somewhere else is yours to clear. Before you pay to run the ad, confirm that placement allows the library track.

faq.q: Can the edit follow the music?
faq.a: Yes. A zipper pull can sit on a beat you chose. If the cuts get so fast that the label blurs, slow the clip down. The product has to stay readable.

faq.q: Can I start from a product page or a short article?
faq.a: Yes. A page that already lists the size and the fabric can supply the spoken line. You can change that line before the job starts. A photo you took of the item is enough when the page is thin.

faq.q: Can I change how the words on screen look?
faq.a: Yes. The words can use your shop's color, and they can sit still instead of bouncing. Set that before you spend the credits.

faq.q: Can the same ad run in another language?
faq.a: Yes. A shop that sells the same kettle in Spanish needs a second file. The scene can stay. The spoken line is the part you replace.

faq.q: Which shape should a small shop make first?
faq.a: 9:16, when the first placement is a full phone screen. Add a square when the same offer also sits in a scrolling feed. Make the wide 16:9 file only when the screen itself is wide.

cta_title: Make the Right Size, Then Post It
cta_lead: You get a file that fills the screen you are buying. Start from a product photo or a product link, and pick 9:16, 1:1, or 16:9.
